books.title: Whose Tracks Are These?
books.art_why: Real animals and their tracks exist today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Animal Visitors How do we know whether an animal has visited a place? One way we know is because it may leave tracks, or marks in the soil. Tracks show where the animal’s body has touched the ground. Let’s find out who has visited us today!
pages.brief: Soft soil beside a woodland path today shows several kinds of animal tracks and marks where feet, paws, or bodies touched the ground. No animal is visible; only the tracks lead across the damp earth.

pages.text: Large Animals A large animal that likes honey made these tracks. This animal is a good climber. It has strong claws for digging up plants, and it eats animals, too. Can you guess who it is?
pages.brief: Large animal tracks pressed into soft soil show strong claw marks near plants, where something has been digging. The tracks are clear and large, but the animal itself is not shown. Nearby ground is disturbed from digging up plants.

pages.text: A black bear made these tracks. Black bears sleep all winter and wake up hungry in the spring.
pages.brief: A black bear stands beside deep tracks in soft soil, its strong paws and claws visible. It is outdoors in spring, awake after sleeping all winter and hungry, with its tracks leading away across the ground.

pages.text: A large animal with hooves made these tracks. This animal can eat ten pounds of leaves, bark, and twigs each day. Can you guess who it is?
pages.brief: Large hoofed tracks are pressed into soft ground beside leaves, bark, and twigs. The tracks are wide and clear, showing where a large animal walked, but the animal is not visible. Leaves and twigs lie nearby on the ground.

pages.text: A deer made these tracks. Male deer grow antlers in the spring and shed them in late winter. Baby deer have spots that disappear when they grow up.
pages.brief: A deer stands beside clear tracks in soft ground. An adult male deer has antlers, and a baby deer nearby has spots. The deer are outdoors in a natural setting, with the tracks showing where they walked.

pages.text: A large, strong cat made these tracks. This hunter runs fast and jumps far. It eats other animals, such as deer, birds, and rabbits. Can you guess who it is?
pages.brief: Large, strong cat tracks are pressed into soft ground, showing clear paw prints. The tracks are wide and deep, but no cat is visible. Nearby ground is open, as if a fast hunter has run and jumped through the area.

pages.text: A mountain lion made these tracks. Adult mountain lions live alone most of the time. Babies must learn to hunt before they can leave their mothers.
pages.brief: An adult mountain lion stands near its large paw tracks in soft ground. It is alone in a natural outdoor setting. The tracks lead across the ground, and the mountain lion's strong body and paws are visible.

pages.text: Small Animals A smart bird made these tracks. It has a curved beak and sharp claws. It hunts at night and eats many kinds of animals. Can you guess who it is?
pages.brief: Small bird tracks are pressed into soft ground, showing thin toes and sharp claw marks. No bird is visible, only the clear tracks. The ground is outdoors at night, with the small prints leading across the soil.

pages.text: An owl made these tracks. It has large yellow eyes and can see well in the dark. It makes a noise called a hoot.
pages.brief: An owl stands near its tracks in soft ground, with large yellow eyes visible. It is outdoors at night, looking alert. The owl's sharp claws and curved beak are visible, and its tracks lead across the ground nearby.

pages.text: A small animal made these tracks. Its tail made the line between the footprints. This animal must run very fast to escape being eaten. Can you guess who it is?
pages.brief: Small animal tracks run across soft ground, with a thin tail line between the footprints. No animal is visible, only the tiny footprints and the line. The tracks look as if a fast runner has passed through, escaping danger.

pages.text: A mouse made these tracks. Mice are food for owls, snakes, and other animals. But this one got away!
pages.brief: A mouse stands near its tiny tracks in soft ground, with a thin tail line between the footprints. The mouse is outdoors in a natural setting and has escaped. The small tracks and tail mark lead across the soil nearby.

pages.text: Whose tracks are these? Many Kinds of Tracks Each kind of animal has its own special tracks. Look for tracks when you are in nature. Have fun finding out who has been visiting!
pages.brief: Many kinds of animal tracks cross soft ground in a natural outdoor place. Large and small footprints and marks show where different animals have visited. The tracks lead in different directions across the soil, ready to be found and compared.

books.title: Dogs at Work
books.art_why: Dogs, people, workplaces and rescue scenes are real and can be photographed.

pages.text: Dogs at Work or or at at.
pages.brief: A group of dogs is shown at work in a simple opening scene, with the animals alert and ready, introducing the idea that dogs can have jobs. The dogs stand in a clear, friendly view.

pages.text: or at at.
pages.brief: A second opening scene shows dogs in work settings, with the animals standing calmly and looking ready, keeping the focus on the general idea of dogs doing jobs. No single job is singled out here; the scene stays simple and broad.

pages.text: Introduction Dogs are not just pets. Some of them have jobs! Dogs learn fast. They hear and smell really well. Dogs can do jobs that people can’t.
pages.brief: Several dogs are shown as pets and as workers, with one dog learning a task, another listening closely, and another sniffing, showing that dogs learn fast, hear and smell well, and can do jobs people cannot.

pages.text: Service and Therapy Dogs Some dogs help people feel calm. These dogs are therapy dogs. Therapy dogs can comfort people who are sick.
pages.brief: A therapy dog sits close to a sick person, helping them feel calm and comforting them in a gentle indoor setting. The dog is calm and friendly, and the person rests nearby as the dog offers comfort.

pages.text: Other dogs help people with These dogs are service dogs. Some help people who can’t see or hear well. Others pick up items and pull wheelchairs.
pages.brief: Service dogs help people who cannot see or hear well, and other service dogs pick up items from the floor or pull a wheelchair, showing different ways these dogs assist their owners. The dogs stay close to the people they help.

pages.text: Dogs have a great sense of smell. Some can smell when their owner is about to be sick. They warn them to take medicine.
pages.brief: A dog sniffs near its owner and senses that the person is about to be sick, then warns the owner by staying close and alert; medicine sits nearby as the owner prepares to take it.

pages.text: Search-and-Rescue Dogs Some dogs look for lost people. They are search-and-rescue dogs. Some smell the ground to find people.
pages.brief: A search-and-rescue dog lowers its nose to the ground in a forest, sniffing for a lost person; the dog works steadily outdoors, using its strong sense of smell to search. The setting is open and natural.

pages.text: Others smell the air. These dogs find lost hikers. They also find people under buildings that fall down.
pages.brief: A search-and-rescue dog lifts its head and smells the air near a trail, finding a lost hiker; nearby, the same kind of dog searches rubble from a fallen building for a person trapped underneath. The scene shows two ways the dogs work.

pages.text: Some search-and-rescue dogs work in the water. They pull people to safety. These dogs need to swim well. Big, strong dogs make good water rescue dogs.
pages.brief: A big, strong search-and-rescue dog swims in the water and pulls a person to safety, showing that water rescue dogs must swim well and that large, powerful dogs are well suited to this job. The person holds on as the dog moves through the water.

pages.text: Funny Jobs Some dogs do funny jobs. One dog worked at an airport. He chased birds away from planes.
pages.brief: At an airport, a dog runs across the open ground and chases birds away from a plane, showing one funny job a dog has done; the dog is active and focused on the birds. The plane stands nearby.

pages.text: Detection Dogs Some dogs use their nose to find hidden things. They are detection dogs. Police use these dogs to find.
pages.brief: A detection dog sniffs around objects to find something hidden, while a police officer stands nearby; the dog uses its nose carefully, showing how police use detection dogs in their work. The dog is alert and focused on the search.

pages.text: These dogs smell buildings after They can smell chemicals. They can tell if someone started a fire on purpose.
pages.brief: A detection dog sniffs inside a building after a fire, checking for chemicals in the air and on surfaces; the dog can help tell whether someone started the fire on purpose. The dog works carefully in the damaged space.

pages.text: Some insects eat wood. They ruin buildings by eating them. Detection dogs can find them before they eat too much.
pages.brief: A detection dog sniffs at wooden beams in a building where small insects are eating the wood; the dog searches carefully so the insects can be found before they ruin too much of the building.

pages.text: Conclusion Dogs do jobs to help us in many ways. They are smart and friendly. They have strong senses. They are some of the best workers around.
pages.brief: Several working dogs are shown together in different jobs, helping people in many ways; they look smart, friendly and alert, with strong senses, making them some of the best workers around. The dogs stand in a clear group view.

books.title: Sharks
books.art_why: Keyword check calls for a drawing, so the shark pages are illustrated.

pages.text: Sharks are fish, but their skeletons are made of cartilage instead of bones Cartilage is what gives human ears their shape Unlike most fish, sharks have rough skin Sharks can sense other animals moving in the water They also see well in the dark Sharks have a good sense of smell .
pages.brief: Underwater, a shark swims, its body made of cartilage instead of bone, with rough skin visible. Beside it, a human ear shows the same cartilage shape. The shark senses other animals moving, sees through dark water, and follows a smell.

pages.text: Description Sharks come in many sizes  Some sharks are only a few inches long The huge whale shark is the largest fish in the world This shading makes it harder for other animals to see them Many sharks are dark on the top and light on the bottom.
pages.brief: In the ocean, a tiny shark only a few inches long swims near the huge whale shark, the largest fish in the world. Both sharks are dark on top and light underneath, which makes them harder for other animals to see.

pages.text: Sharks swim by swinging their tails from side to side Fins help sharks steer, turn, and keep their balance to take its place When one tooth breaks off, another one moves up Most sharks have many rows of teeth Eating Do You Know? A shark may wear out and regrow a thousand teeth during its lifetime.
pages.brief: A shark swims by swinging its tail from side to side. Its fins help it steer, turn, and keep balance. In its open mouth, many rows of teeth are visible; when one tooth breaks off, another moves up to take its place. A shark may wear out and regrow a thousand teeth in its lifetime.

pages.text: Do You Know? A great white shark can swallow a whole seal in one gulp. Most sharks eat fish  Large sharks eat sea lions, dolphins, and other sharks Some sharks eat shellfish These sharks have flat teeth for crushing shells that float near the ocean’s surface   It swallows very small ocean plants and animals use them when eating   The huge whale shark has tiny teeth but doesn’t.
pages.brief: A great white shark swallows a whole seal in one gulp. Nearby, sharks eat fish, and large sharks eat sea lions, dolphins, and other sharks. A shellfish-crushing shark shows flat teeth, while the whale shark swallows tiny ocean plants and animals near the surface.

pages.text: Many people are afraid of sharks, but most sharks do not attack humans  Great white sharks are one of the few kinds of sharks that are dangerous to people Many people eat shark meat, and shark fins are used to make soup Shark Attacks People hunt sharks for their skin, oil, and teeth Shark Hunting.
pages.brief: A great white shark swims in the ocean while people nearby look afraid, but most sharks do not attack humans. Other people eat shark meat and use shark fins for soup. Some people hunt sharks for their skin, oil, and teeth.

pages.text: Many kinds of sharks are now in danger of being completely killed off  Sharks are an important part of the balance of life in the world’s oceans They have as much right to live as any other animal the part of the ocean or land that touches the air above it surface (n.) page 12 to turn to move in a desired direction a group of reptiles that lived long ago an elastic tissue that makes up the skeletons of sharks, and rays Glossary.
pages.brief: Many sharks swim together in the world’s oceans, some near the surface. They are shown as an important part of the balance of life in the ocean, with as much right to live as any other animal.

books.title: Heroes of September 11
books.art_why: Real photographs exist of the September 11, 2001 emergency and its helpers.

pages.text: Heroes of September 11.
pages.brief: The opening page is plain and uncluttered, with a calm, serious background. No people, buildings, or objects appear. It leaves space for the book's opening information and sets a respectful tone before the true story begins.

pages.text: Emergency New York City faced an emergency on September 11, 2001. Planes hit two huge buildings. The buildings caught fire. People inside needed to get out. Hurt people needed to find doctors. The fire left a mess that was not safe. Many brave heroes stepped in to help.
pages.brief: Two huge buildings stand in New York City, struck by planes and burning. Smoke rises, and people inside need to get out. Hurt people look for doctors. The fire leaves unsafe mess. Many brave helpers step in to assist.

pages.text: Office Workers The burning buildings filled with smoke. It wasn’t safe to use the elevators. People rushed down the stairs.
pages.brief: Inside a burning building, thick smoke fills the air. Office workers avoid the elevators and rush down the stairs. They move quickly through the smoky stairwell, helping each other get out. The stairs are crowded with people leaving.

pages.text: Two men saw a woman in a wheelchair on floor 68. They saw she needed help, so the men carried her to safety. Many office workers stopped to help others that day.
pages.brief: On a high floor, two men see a woman in a wheelchair who needs help. They carry her to safety down the stairs. Around them, many office workers stop to help other people get out of the building.

pages.text: Dogs Not all the heroes were people. Some were dogs. About 400 dogs helped that day. Some dogs looked for hurt and lost people to rescue. Some dogs just helped people feel better.
pages.brief: About 400 dogs help at the emergency site. Some dogs search for hurt and lost people to rescue. Other dogs sit with people and help them feel better. The dogs work alongside people, showing that heroes can have four legs.

pages.text: One dog was inside when the fire started. She helped her owner, a blind office worker. The dog led her owner down to safety from floor 78!
pages.brief: One dog is inside a burning building when the fire starts. The dog helps her owner, a blind office worker. The dog leads her owner down the stairs from a high floor to safety. The dog stays close and guides the way.

pages.text: Firefighters Firefighters raced to the burning buildings and ran inside. They put themselves in danger to save others.
pages.brief: Firefighters race to the burning buildings. Wearing heavy gear, they run inside the smoky towers. They put themselves in danger to save other people, moving toward the fire while everyone else tries to get out.

pages.text: Other firefighters cleared the area around the burning buildings. They moved everyone away from danger.
pages.brief: Other firefighters work outside the burning buildings. They clear the area and move everyone away from danger. They guide people back, keeping them at a safer distance from the falling debris and fire. Their job is to keep the crowd out of harm's way.

pages.text: Firefighters looked for people to rescue. They found lost people and took hurt ones to doctors.
pages.brief: Firefighters search the smoky ruins for people to rescue. They find lost people and lead them out. They take hurt people to doctors for care, working carefully in the dangerous area around the burning buildings.

pages.text: Ironworkers The burned buildings fell down. Piles of broken walls and floors lay everywhere. These ruins were not safe.
pages.brief: The burned buildings have fallen down. Piles of broken walls and floors lie everywhere. The ruins are not safe, with twisted debris and uneven ground. The scene is dangerous for anyone who comes near. The wreckage stretches across the area.

pages.text: Ironworkers came from all over to help. Ironworkers are builders. Some of them had built the buildings that burned.
pages.brief: Ironworkers come from all over to help. These builders wear work gear and arrive at the ruins. Some of them had built the buildings that burned. They look at the piles of broken walls and floors, ready to begin the hard cleanup.

pages.text: The ironworkers had to work with care to clean up the ruins. They put themselves in danger every day until the mess was safe.
pages.brief: Ironworkers clean up the ruins with care. They move broken walls and floors, watching for danger as they work. They put themselves in danger every day until the mess is safe. The work is slow and careful.

pages.text: Help in Hard Times This emergency showed how brave people and dogs can be. They faced danger to keep others safe. Sometimes they felt afraid, but fear didn‘t stop these heroes from helping others.
pages.brief: Brave people and dogs stand together after the emergency. They faced danger to keep others safe. Some felt afraid, but fear did not stop them from helping. The group shows courage and kindness in hard times.

books.title: A Rainbow of Food
books.art_why: Fruits and vegetables are real everyday foods that can be photographed.

pages.text: A Rainbow w of Food of Food.
pages.brief: A bright display of colorful fruits and vegetables arranged in a rainbow arc, with red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple foods grouped in clear bands. The foods sit against a clean, simple background, inviting young readers into the book.

pages.text: Did you know that you can eat a rainbow? You can’t eat a rainbow in the sky, of course. You can make a healthy rainbow out of all the different colors of fruits and vegetables.
pages.brief: A sky rainbow arcs above a colorful spread of fruits and vegetables in many colors. Below the sky rainbow, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple produce are gathered together, showing the healthy food rainbow on a simple bright background.

pages.text: A red apple can help keep your heart strong. Eat some slices of this fruit for a healthy snack.
pages.brief: A shiny red apple sits whole beside several crisp apple slices arranged as a healthy snack. The fruit is shown in a clean, simple setting, with the whole apple and slices clearly visible so readers can see the red color and snack-ready pieces.

pages.text: Red raspberries can help keep you from getting sick. Eat a handful of this fruit instead of candy.
pages.brief: A small handful of bright red raspberries is held up, with the tiny berries clustered together. The simple, clean background keeps attention on the raspberries as a healthy fruit choice for a snack.

pages.text: An orange carrot can help keep your eyes healthy. This vegetable is just plain fun to crunch between your teeth.
pages.brief: A bright orange carrot stands whole beside several carrot sticks, shown crisp and ready to crunch. The vegetable is set against a clean, simple background, with the orange color clear and the crunchy sticks easy to see as a healthy snack.

pages.text: An orange is filled with vitamins that can help keep you from catching a cold. Squeeze this fruit for some tangy juice with breakfast in the morning.
pages.brief: A whole orange sits beside a glass of fresh orange juice, with a cut orange half showing juicy segments. The morning breakfast scene is simple and bright, focusing on the fruit and the tangy juice squeezed for breakfast.

pages.text: A yellow banana can give you tons of energy. Peel and eat this fruit before you play.
pages.brief: A bright yellow banana is shown partly peeled, with the soft fruit ready to eat. The banana rests against a clean, simple background, suggesting a quick energy snack before play without adding other objects or people.

pages.text: Yellow corn can help keep your stomach healthy. Munch this vegetable right off the cob at.
pages.brief: A bright yellow ear of corn on the cob is shown with kernels ready to munch. The corn sits in a clean, simple setting, with the yellow color and cob shape clear, illustrating a healthy vegetable to eat right off the cob.

pages.text: A green avocado can help your body take in all the stuff it needs. Squish up this fruit to make a creamy dip for chips.
pages.brief: A green avocado is shown cut open beside a bowl of creamy avocado dip and a few chips. The simple, bright scene focuses on the creamy dip made by squishing the fruit, with the green avocado clearly visible.

pages.text: Green broccoli can help keep your bones strong. Pretend you are a dinosaur eating a tree and chow down on this vegetable.
pages.brief: A child pretends to be a dinosaur, leaning toward a piece of green broccoli held like a little tree. The playful scene is simple and bright, focusing on the broccoli as a crunchy vegetable to chow down.

pages.text: Blueberries can help you remember things. Eat this fruit every day to help you do well in school.
pages.brief: A small pile of bright blueberries sits in a clean, simple setting, shown as an everyday fruit to eat. The blueberries are clearly visible, with their deep blue color standing out against a plain background.

pages.text: Purple plums help food move through your body. Get sticky with a bite of this juicy fruit.
pages.brief: A ripe purple plum is shown whole beside a cut plum with juicy, sticky flesh. The simple, clean scene focuses on the fruit’s purple color and juicy inside, making it look ready for a bite.

pages.text: Purple grapes can help keep blood moving around your body. Toss a bunch of this fruit in the freezer and have a chilly treat.
pages.brief: A bunch of purple grapes is shown with a few frozen grapes nearby, looking like a chilly treat. The simple, clean scene focuses on the grapes, with their purple color clear and the frozen fruit ready to enjoy.

pages.text: These fruits and vegetables are just a few that can make up a food rainbow. Eating a rainbow every day is a fun and colorful way to stay healthy. How many colors will you eat today?
pages.brief: A colorful spread of fruits and vegetables from the book is arranged like a food rainbow, with red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple foods visible. The bright, simple scene invites readers to count the colors they might eat today.

books.title: Want to Be a Beaver?
books.art_why: Keyword check suggests drawing, and the text does not clearly require photographs.

pages.text: Want to Be a Beaver?
pages.brief: A beaver stands beside calm water, looking toward the viewer. Its brown fur, flat tail and small ears are visible. Soft natural light and green plants frame the scene, and the beaver appears calm and curious. The water reflects the surrounding greenery.

pages.text: Beaver? Want to Be a.
pages.brief: A beaver swims through clear water, its body moving below the surface. Ripples spread above it, and the pond is calm and open. The beaver’s flat tail trails behind as it glides forward. Green banks are visible beyond the water.

pages.text: Do you like to play in water? Do you like to swim? If you do, then you might like life.
pages.brief: A beaver plays and swims in clear water, its body rolling through ripples. The water surrounds it, inviting the viewer to imagine liking water and swimming. The beaver looks at home in the pond, with a calm surface and soft reflected light.

pages.text: When you’re a beaver, you can swim days after being born. As an adult, you can hold your breath for fifteen minutes.
pages.brief: A tiny newborn beaver swims beside an adult in clear water, only days old. The adult beaver glides underwater, holding its breath. Both have brown fur and small ears, and the water surrounds them as they move together.

pages.text: A set of clear eyelids allows you to see underwater. You can also close your nose and ears to keep out water. Do You Know? Beavers are not as big as they used to be. Long ago, beavers in North America were more than 8 feet (2.5 m) long–larger than a black bear today!
pages.brief: A beaver swims underwater with its clear eyelids closed over its eyes and its nose and ears shut against the water. Nearby, an ancient beaver is shown longer than a black bear, while a modern beaver looks smaller. The water is clear around them.

pages.text: Your four huge front teeth never stop growing! Chewing on wood all the time keeps them from growing too long. You can chew through a skinny tree in twenty minutes.
pages.brief: A beaver presses its four huge front teeth into a skinny tree trunk. Wood chips scatter as it chews, and the tree leans slightly. The beaver’s teeth are visible and long, working steadily on the wood. The scene is set near the water’s edge with the tree between beaver and pond.

pages.text: Why do you want to chew through Dandy Dams In a week, a beaver family can build a dam that is 35 feet (10.7 m) long. Some dams, built over many years, have been more than 1,000 feet (305 m) long! Beaver dams create ponds, which provide a place to live for many plants as well as fish, turtles, frogs, birds, and other animals. Humans dislike the dams, though, when they flood human homes and farmland.
pages.brief: A beaver family works together on a long dam of sticks and mud across a stream. Behind the dam a pond spreads out, with fish, turtles, frogs, birds and plants nearby. In the distance, people look unhappy as water floods homes and farmland.

pages.text: Behind the dam, you build your A lodge is shaped like a dome and made of sticks and mud. In cold weather, the mud freezes hard. This keeps the lodge warm. Look Inside a Lodge underwater entrances.
pages.brief: A dome-shaped lodge of sticks and mud sits behind the dam at the water’s edge. A cutaway view shows the inside, with underwater entrances leading up into the warm lodge. In cold weather the mud is frozen hard on the outside, while the inner space stays protected.

pages.text: Your family, called a colony, lives in the lodge together. You and your mate stay together for many years.
pages.brief: Inside the lodge, a beaver colony rests together. The adult pair sits close, staying together for many years, while younger beavers share the warm space. Sticks and mud form the dome around them, and the dark interior feels sheltered. The family is gathered in the lodge as a group.

pages.text: As a beaver, you waste nothing. You eat the leaves, twigs, and bark of the trees you cut down. You store enough limbs under the water near your lodge to last all winter.
pages.brief: A beaver eats leaves, twigs and bark from a fallen tree it has cut down. Nearby, limbs are tucked underwater beside the lodge, stored for winter. The beaver uses the tree fully, wasting nothing, while the pond holds the supply below the surface.

pages.text: In the spring, you dine on ferns and water plants. You fill up on roots, too.
pages.brief: In spring, a beaver feeds among ferns and water plants at the pond’s edge. It pulls up roots and eats them, filling up on fresh green growth. The water is calm, and the plants surround the beaver as it dines. The scene shows the beaver’s spring food.

pages.text: Storing food and working on your dam keeps you busy. You work mostly at night because you are nocturnal. Do You Know? When people work hard, we say they are “busy as a beaver.”
pages.brief: At night, a beaver works on its dam, carrying sticks and patching the mud. The moonlit pond is dark, and the beaver stays busy storing food and repairing the structure. Its flat tail trails behind as it moves along the dam. The scene shows nighttime work.

pages.text: Some animals hunt you because you’re slow on land. You’re safe in the water, though. When an enemy comes close, you slap the water with your flat, wide tail. The loud sound may warn other beavers.
pages.brief: A beaver swims in the pond while an enemy approaches from the shore. The beaver is slow on land but safe in the water. It slaps the surface with its flat, wide tail, sending up a loud splash that warns other beavers nearby.

pages.text: Your tail also helps you balance when you stand. It helps you steer when you swim. It even stores fat for the winter.
pages.brief: A beaver stands upright with its wide tail pressed to the ground for balance. In the water, the same tail angles to steer as the beaver swims. The tail is thick and flat, storing fat for the winter. The scene shows the tail’s three uses.

pages.text: If you like water and don’t mind work, then you might like being Beavers Live Here.
pages.brief: A beaver sits beside a pond in a watery habitat, near sticks and mud from its work. The scene shows the beaver living where there is water and plenty to do. Reeds and trees surround the pond, and the beaver looks settled in its home.

books.title: Mexico
books.art_why: The keyword check flagged the historical celebration pages (Day of the Dead, the old fight for freedom), and illustration carries the mix of old and new well.

pages.text: Where Is It? Mexico is a country in North America. To the north of it is the United States. To the south of it is Central America. To the east and west of Mexico is the sea.
pages.brief: A high view of the North American landmass from above: Mexico in the centre, the United States stretching away to the north, Central America to the south, and wide blue sea running along Mexico's eastern and western coasts. Green and brown land, a few white clouds, bright sunlight.

pages.text: More than 120 million people live in Mexico. Most of them live in cities.
pages.brief: A crowded city street in Mexico. Many people walk, shop and talk along the pavement, with tall buildings behind them, cars and buses on the road, and rows of rooftops spreading far into the distance where more families live.

pages.text: The capital of Mexico is Mexico City. It is one of the oldest cities in North America. It also has more people than any other city in North America!
pages.brief: Mexico City seen from a wide avenue: an old stone plaza with a cathedral on one side, tall modern towers behind, and thick crowds of people crossing the open square. Older low buildings and newer high ones stand close together under a bright sky.

pages.text: People Most people in Mexico speak Spanish. More people speak Spanish in Mexico than anywhere else.
pages.brief: People in Mexico talking together in Spanish: a family chatting around a courtyard table, a market seller calling to a customer, two friends laughing on a doorstep. Warm colourful houses and hanging plants behind them, everyday city life around.

pages.text: Land Mountains and canyons cover much of Mexico. Dry deserts are in the north. Forests cover land to the south. Two pieces of land stretch into the ocean. Baja (BAH-hah) is like a long finger. Yucatán (yoo-kah-TAHN) is more like a thumb.
pages.brief: A wide sweep of Mexican land: rocky mountains and deep canyons inland, dry pale desert in the north, dense green forest in the south, and two long arms of land reaching into the blue ocean — one thin and finger-like, the other short and thumb-shaped.

pages.text: Animals Many different animals call Mexico home. Parrots, frogs, and many other animals live in the hot, wet forests. Foxes, lizards, and other animals live in the hot, dry deserts.
pages.brief: Two habitats side by side. In a hot, wet green forest, bright parrots perch on branches while frogs sit on leaves near a pool. In a hot, dry desert of sand and cactus, a fox stands alert and a lizard rests on a warm rock.

pages.text: Celebrations People in Mexico celebrate many special days. The Day of the Dead lasts three days. It is a happy time. People remember their loved ones. They light candles and wear masks.
pages.brief: A family celebrating the Day of the Dead indoors and in a courtyard at dusk: candles glowing on a table, people wearing painted masks, marigold flowers around them, everyone gathered happily to remember loved ones.

pages.text: People also remember the day long ago when Mexico began its fight to be free. They dress up and walk in parades. They light fireworks to celebrate.
pages.brief: A street parade: people dressed in bright costumes and hats walking together along a road, waving and smiling, crowds watching from the sides, and fireworks bursting in the evening sky above the rooftops.

pages.text: Food Corn is an important food in Mexico. It is in almost every meal. People in Mexico also eat parts of cactus. They eat chicken and pork. Some people eat food from the sea.
pages.brief: A Mexican meal laid out on a table: corn cobs and corn dishes, sliced cactus, cooked chicken and pork, and a plate of food from the sea. Hands reaching to serve, a warm kitchen or market stall behind.

pages.text: People in Mexico often use peppers in their food. Some peppers are hot, like chile (CHIH-lee) peppers. Some peppers just make food taste different.
pages.brief: A close view of peppers on a market stall: small fiery chile peppers piled in a basket, larger mild peppers beside them, and a cook sprinkling chopped pepper over food in a pan, steam rising.

pages.text: Conclusion Mexico is an exciting country. Many different people and animals live there. What is your favorite thing about Mexico?
pages.brief: A lively outdoor scene in Mexico: children and adults together in a green square, a parrot on a branch above them, a lizard on a wall, mountains in the distance. Everyone smiling, looking around at the country they live in.

books.title: Brazil
books.art_why: Brazil exists today and can be shown in real photographs.

pages.text: Brazil Where Is It? Brazil is the biggest country in South America. It covers almost half of the.
pages.brief: A wide view of Brazil’s land in South America, showing the country taking up almost half of the continent. The land stretches far across the scene, with open space and natural ground visible from a distance.

pages.text: Other countries border it to the north, south, and west. The Atlantic Ocean is to the east. The capital city of Brazil is Brasília (bruh-ZIL-yuh). Brasília became the capital in 1960. The city was built to be the capital. It was built in only a few years.
pages.brief: A view of Brasília, the capital city of Brazil, built in only a few years and made the capital in 1960. The Atlantic Ocean lies to the east, while other countries border the land to the north, south and west.

pages.text: People More than two hundred million people live in Brazil. Most people in Brazil speak Portuguese (POR-chuh-geez).
pages.brief: A busy scene of Brazil’s people, more than two hundred million living across the country. A group of people of different ages stand together in a Brazilian city or town, speaking Portuguese as their main language.

pages.text: Most people in Brazil live in cities. Many of these cities are on the coast. Some people live in the country.
pages.brief: Many people in Brazil are shown living in cities along the coast, with buildings and streets near the ocean. A smaller group is shown in the countryside, where fewer people live among open land.

pages.text: Brazil has many different kinds of land. It has beaches and tall mountains. It also has flat land covered with water. Brazil Land.
pages.brief: Different kinds of Brazilian land appear together: sandy beaches, tall mountains, and flat land covered with water. The scene shows the varied landscape of Brazil, from the coast to high peaks and wet flat areas.

pages.text: Brazil is home to the Amazon It covers almost half of Brazil. It is the biggest rainforest in the world. The Amazon River runs through the rainforest. It is one of the longest rivers in the world.
pages.brief: The Amazon rainforest covers almost half of Brazil, with the Amazon River running through it. Dense green trees fill the view, and the wide river winds among them, showing one of the world’s longest rivers inside the biggest rainforest.

pages.text: Celebrations People in Brazil celebrate Carnaval. The holiday happens during Brazil’s summer. It goes on for four days.
pages.brief: People in Brazil celebrate Carnaval during Brazil’s summer. A festive street or square is filled with people enjoying the holiday, which goes on for four days, with groups gathering together for the celebration.

pages.text: People dress up and walk in big parades. People play many different kinds of music. The party is one of the biggest in the world.
pages.brief: People dress up and walk in big parades, playing many different kinds of music. A lively parade fills the street with costumed people moving together, musicians playing instruments, and a large crowd enjoying one of the biggest parties in the world.

pages.text: Animals Many animals live in the Amazon rainforest. Parrots live there. They have colorful feathers. Colorful frogs live there, too. They live on the ground and in the trees.
pages.brief: Parrots with colorful feathers live in the Amazon rainforest, shown perched in the trees. Colorful frogs live there too, shown on the ground and among the trees, sharing the rainforest with the birds.

pages.text: Many ants live in the rainforest. Fire ants and leaf-cutter ants live there. Many spiders live in the rainforest, too. The biggest spider in the world lives there.
pages.brief: Many ants live in the rainforest, including fire ants and leaf-cutter ants moving along the ground. Many spiders live there too, and the biggest spider in the world is shown among the leaves and forest floor.

pages.text: Conclusion Brazil is an exciting country. It has big cities. It has forests filled with many animals. What do you like most about Brazil?
pages.brief: A final view of Brazil shows big cities and forests filled with many animals. Exciting scenes from across the country come together, inviting the reader to think about what they like most about Brazil.

books.title: Egypt
books.art_why: The book covers ancient pharaohs, pyramids and tomb treasures from long before photographs.

pages.text: Where Is It? Egypt is a country in North Africa. The Mediterranean (MEH-duh-tuh- RAY-nee-uhn) Sea is to the north. The Red Sea is to the east. Other countries are to the west and south.
pages.brief: A wide desert view of North Africa showing Egypt's land: the Mediterranean Sea stretches along the top to the north, the Red Sea lies to the east on the right, and dry desert countries spread to the west and south. Sand, rocky ground and blue water meet under a clear sky.

pages.text: The capital city of Egypt is Cairo (KEYE-roh). It is also one of the largest cities in Africa. More than twenty-one million people live there.
pages.brief: A busy Cairo street crowded with people walking past tall buildings, shops and balconies. Many Egyptians of all ages fill the pavement, some carrying bags, others talking. Cars and buses wait in the road behind them. The city stretches far into the distance under a warm sky.

pages.text: People More than 106 million people live in Egypt. Most of them speak Arabic. Many people live in farming towns along the Nile River.
pages.brief: Families in a farming town beside the Nile River, with small mud-brick houses and palm trees. People talk together in Arabic while children play near the water. Green fields run along the riverbank, and a few villagers carry baskets. Warm sunlight falls on the wide, slow river.

pages.text: Some farmers in Egypt grow cotton along the Nile. The cotton is used to make clothes. Farmers also grow rice, wheat, and other foods.
pages.brief: Farmers bending over rows of cotton plants in a field beside the Nile, white cotton bolls open on the stems. One farmer holds a full basket. Behind them, neat plots of rice and wheat grow green. Palm trees and the shining river lie at the edge of the field under a bright sky.

pages.text: Land The desert stretches across all of Egypt. The Nile River runs through the east. It is the longest river in the world.
pages.brief: Endless sandy desert stretching across Egypt, with dunes and rocky hills. To the east, the wide Nile River winds through the dry land, its green banks standing out against the sand. A few palm trees line the water. The desert reaches far to the horizon under a hot sky.

pages.text: The Nile ends at the Mediterranean Sea. The land where the Nile ends is the Nile Delta.
pages.brief: The Nile spreading out into many channels as it meets the Mediterranean Sea, forming a wide green delta of fields and reeds. Water flows between islands of farmland, and the blue sea opens beyond. Birds fly over the marshy edges, and small boats rest near the shore.

pages.text: Egypt also has mountains. Tall mountains rise in the east. Low mountains rise in the west.
pages.brief: A mountain landscape in Egypt: tall rocky peaks rising in the east on one side, and lower, rounded mountains stretching west on the other. Dry slopes and stony valleys lie between them, with a little scrub. Shadows fall across the ridges under a pale sky.

pages.text: Animals Many animals live in Egypt. Foxes, lizards, and other animals live in the desert. Some people raise water buffalo, sheep, and goats. Some people use camels to travel from place to place.
pages.brief: A desert scene with a small fox and a lizard near rocks and sand. Nearby, a farmer tends water buffalo, sheep and goats in a pen. A camel carrying a rider walks along a dusty path between them, and palm trees stand in the distance.

pages.text: History Egypt is very old. Long ago, kings called pharaohs (FEHR-ohz) ruled the land. Some people believed the pharaohs were gods.
pages.brief: An ancient Egyptian pharaoh seated on a throne, wearing a striped headdress and holding a staff, while people bow before him. Temple pillars and painted walls stand behind. Attendants raise their hands in respect, and sunlight streams through the doorway of the great hall.

pages.text: The pharaohs had huge pyramids (PIHR-uh-midz) built. These pyramids are tombs for the pharaohs. Gold treasures were placed in the tombs. Some of these treasures are in museums now.
pages.brief: A huge stone pyramid rising from desert sand, with small figures of workers below. Beside it, a cutaway shows a torch-lit tomb chamber holding a golden coffin and shining treasures. In the distance a museum building stands, where some of the gold objects are kept.

pages.text: Conclusion Egypt is an amazing country. It is also a very old country. Egypt has many important things to learn about.
pages.brief: A sweeping view of Egypt today: the crowded city of Cairo, green farm fields along the Nile, wide desert and distant mountains. People walk, farmers work, and boats move on the river. Ancient pyramids stand on the horizon, showing a country both old and modern.

books.title: Why Do Leaves Change Color?
books.art_why: The book explains real trees, leaves, animals, and seasons that can be photographed in nature.

pages.text: So Many Colors Why are the leaves on trees different colors? What makes them change color?
pages.brief: A close view of several tree leaves in different colors—green, yellow, orange, and red—on branches against a bright outdoor background. The leaves are the main subject, showing the color differences among leaves on trees.

pages.text: Two Types of Trees Not all trees lose their leaves in fall. Deciduous (dee-SIJ-oo- us) trees lose their leaves once each year. Evergreen trees lose and grow their leaves throughout the year. This book is about deciduous trees.
pages.brief: A split outdoor scene: on one side, a deciduous tree with leaves turning color and some falling to the ground; on the other, an evergreen tree with green leaves still on its branches. Both trees stand in a natural landscape.

pages.text: Making Food Leaves use sunlight, water, and air to make food for the tree. This way of making food is called helps leaves make food also makes them green.
pages.brief: Sunlight shines onto green leaves on a tree branch, with water droplets on the leaves and open outdoor space around the branch. The leaves are making food for the tree, and their green color is visible.

pages.text: Photosynthesis is important to animals as well as plants. Some animals eat plants. Other animals eat those animals. Without photosynthesis, neither kind of animal would have food.
pages.brief: A plant-eating animal eats green leaves from a plant. Nearby, a meat-eating animal stands near that plant-eating animal. The scene shows animals depending on plants and on other animals for food in a natural outdoor setting.

pages.text: Summer Summer is playtime. For the leaves of many trees, however, it’s work, work, work! The Sun is shining. The leaves are making food for the trees. The trees store any extra food deep inside. The stored food will help them get through winter.
pages.brief: A leafy tree stands under a bright summer sun. Green leaves on its branches are making food, while deep inside the trunk the tree stores extra food. The scene is warm and sunny, showing summer as a busy time for leaves.

pages.text: Leaves are green in summer because they are making food. Leaves also have orange, yellow, or brown colors inside them. During summer, those other colors are hidden by the green color. Do You Know? The same chemical that makes leaves orange is also found in carrots, tomatoes, and sweet potatoes. The same chemical that makes leaves red is also found in berries, cherries, plums, and red cabbage.
pages.brief: Green leaves on a tree branch in summer, with a few leaves partly showing orange, yellow, or brown underneath the green. Nearby, carrots, tomatoes, sweet potatoes, berries, cherries, plums, and red cabbage are arranged to show the same color chemicals.

pages.text: Fall Many places get colder in fall. The days get shorter, and the nights get longer. Trees get less sunlight, so photosynthesis slows down.
pages.brief: An outdoor fall scene with a tree whose leaves are still green, under weaker sunlight. The day is shorter, with less light reaching the tree. The tree receives less sunlight, so its food-making slows down.

pages.text: Over time, leaves stop making the green chemical, so they lose their green color. When that happens, the hidden orange, yellow, and brown colors start to show. Leaves also start making a red color at this time.
pages.brief: Leaves on a branch are losing their green color. Orange, yellow, and brown colors begin to show on the leaves, and some leaves are turning red. The branch is outdoors in fall, with the changing colors clear on each leaf.

pages.text: Once it gets cold enough to freeze at night, the trees drop their leaves. They do this to keep themselves safe. If the leaves freeze while still on the trees, the trees can be hurt.
pages.brief: A cold fall night outdoors, with a tree and its leaves in freezing air. The tree is dropping its leaves, and some leaves have already fallen to the ground. The tree is keeping itself safe by letting the leaves go.

pages.text: Winter Trees that drop their leaves are bare in winter. They use the stored food to get through the cold days and colder nights.
pages.brief: A bare deciduous tree stands outdoors in winter, without leaves on its branches. Cold ground and a winter landscape surround it. Inside the tree, stored food is helping it survive the cold days and colder nights.

pages.text: Spring Spring comes before long. Ice and snow melt, and the rains come. The Sun shines, and tiny leaves grow from branches.
pages.brief: A spring outdoor scene: ice and snow are melting, rain falls, and the sun shines. Tiny new leaves are growing from the branches of a tree. The ground looks wet from rain, and the tree is beginning its new growth.

pages.text: Once again, the leaves use sunlight, water, and air to make food. The cycle begins again.
pages.brief: Green leaves on a tree branch use sunlight, water, and air to make food. The tree stands outdoors in daylight, and the leaves are growing again as the cycle repeats. Sunlight reaches the branch, water is near the leaves, and air surrounds them.

books.title: Ostriches: Giant Birds
books.art_why: Ostriches and African savanna exist today and are photographed easily.

pages.text: A Very Big Bird The ostrich is the biggest bird in the world. Most ostriches are taller than the tallest people.
pages.brief: A single adult ostrich stands tall on open African grassland, its long bare neck stretched up and its feathery body filling the frame beside a tall person so the bird clearly looks taller. Dry grass and a few low bushes spread behind it under bright daylight.

pages.text: Ostriches have wings and feathers, but they can’t fly. An ostrich can run fast and far. It is the fastest animal with two legs. It runs faster than most four-legged animals.
pages.brief: An ostrich sprints across dusty savanna ground, wings slightly spread and long legs stretched out mid-stride, feathers flying. Behind it a trailing cloud of dust shows how fast it moves as it passes low grass and scattered stones.

pages.text: Eyes on the Prize Ostriches have small heads with big eyes. Their eyes are bigger than those of any other land animal.
pages.brief: A close-up of an ostrich's small head on its long thin neck, turned toward the viewer. One enormous dark eye with thick lashes fills much of the head, catching the light, with soft blurred grassland behind the feathery neck and beak.

pages.text: Ostrich range AFRICA Ostrich range Home, Sweet Home Most wild ostriches live in Africa. They live in small herds of ten or more birds.
pages.brief: A simple view of African savanna: dry golden grass, scattered acacia trees and a wide sky. A small herd of ostriches, ten or more grey-brown and black birds, walks together across the plain, some bending to peck at the ground.

pages.text: Ostriches use teamwork to stay safe. Their sharp eyes and long necks help them spot danger from far away.
pages.brief: Several ostriches stand together in a loose group on open grassland, all with heads raised high on long necks, looking in different directions across the plain. Their upright, alert posture shows the birds watching the wide land around them.

pages.text: What’s on the Menu? Ostriches eat grass, other plants, and fruit. They also eat bugs and other small animals. Ostriches don’t drink much water. They get water from the plants and fruit they eat.
pages.brief: An ostrich bends its long neck down to the ground, cropping green grass and leaves, with red fruit and small insects on the soil nearby. Low shrubs and dry plants surround it on the sunny African savanna.

pages.text: Look Out! Run! Lions and cheetahs hunt ostriches for food. Ostriches must be on the lookout. Their long necks help them look far. They have strong legs and big feet. An ostrich can kick very hard. Its kick can kill a lion.
pages.brief: An ostrich faces a lion on open ground, wings out and one powerful leg raised in a hard kick, its big foot aimed forward. The lion is close and low, and a cheetah stands further off in the grass behind them.

pages.text: Ostriches make a loud noise when they see a lion. The noise warns other animals that lions are near.
pages.brief: An ostrich stands with its neck stretched high and its beak wide open, making a loud call across the savanna. In the distance a lion walks through tall grass, and nearby other grazing animals lift their heads.

pages.text: From Big Egg to Big Bird A male ostrich digs a shallow pit in the dirt for a nest. The mother lays her eggs in the pit. In six weeks, baby ostriches hatch from the eggs. A baby ostrich is the size of a grown chicken.
pages.brief: On bare ground, a shallow pit nest holds a cluster of huge cream-white eggs. A male ostrich stands over it on the dirt while the female is nearby, and one tiny chick stands beside the eggs, small as a grown chicken.

pages.text: An ostrich chick grows about 1 foot (30 cm) per month. In six months, the baby ostrich will be grown. It can live for fifty years or more.
pages.brief: A young ostrich chick with fluffy striped down stands on the savanna beside a full-grown adult ostrich, showing how much taller the adult is. Both stand in bright sunlight on dry grass with low bushes behind.

pages.text: Conclusion Ostriches are special birds. They are strong and fast. Ostriches are bigger than any other bird.
pages.brief: A big adult ostrich stands on the open African plain with its head high, wings slightly out and strong legs planted. Wide grassland and distant trees stretch behind it, with a few other ostriches walking far away.

books.title: Goliath Beetles: Giant Insects
books.art_why: Goliath beetles are real living insects that can be photographed today.

pages.text: The World’s Biggest Beetle Goliath beetles are the giants of the insect world. Adult Goliaths can be bigger than a songbird. A young Goliath beetle A larva can be even bigger than an adult beetle!
pages.brief: A large adult Goliath beetle with black and white stripes clings to a tree trunk, its body longer than the small songbird perched on a nearby branch. Beside them a thick white larva curls on the forest floor, bigger than the adult beetle.

pages.text: What Is a Beetle? All beetles have two sets of wings. The large wings in the back are for flying. The front wings are smaller and harder. They protect the flying wings.
pages.brief: A Goliath beetle seen from above on a leaf, its hard front wings lifted open. Underneath, the thin back wings spread wide for flying. The smaller, tougher outer wings rest partly over the folded flying wings.

pages.text: Beetles have mouths that help them chew. Some insects, like butterflies, have mouths like straws. Other insects have mouths like needles.
pages.brief: Close view of a Goliath beetle's chewing mouthparts biting into a piece of fruit. Nearby a butterfly unrolls a long straw-like mouth to sip from a flower, and another insect with a thin needle-like mouth rests on a stem.

pages.text: Little Zebras Most Goliath beetles have black stripes. Some beetles are plain brown. No two beetles are the same. People once called Goliath beetles “zebra beetles” because of their stripes.
pages.brief: Three Goliath beetles on a tree trunk, each with different markings: one with bold black stripes on white, one with faint stripes, and one plain brown. All three have the same rounded bodies and small horns.

pages.text: An African Home Goliath beetles live in forests and grassy parts of Africa.
pages.brief: A wide view of an African landscape where forest trees and open grassy patches meet. A Goliath beetle walks across the grass near the edge of the trees, sunlight falling through the leaves above.

pages.text: They are only seen during the rainy time of year. That’s when there is plenty of fruit for them to eat. Male Goliath beetles fight other males over feeding places. Male beetles may get mates by having good feeding places.
pages.brief: In heavy rain, two male Goliath beetles push and butt heads on a tree trunk beside a pile of ripe fruit. A female beetle waits nearby on the bark, raindrops falling and wet leaves shining around them.

pages.text: Big Changes Female Goliath beetles put their eggs in a deep hole. Larvae hatch about two weeks later. The larvae eat dead plants in the soil and grow fast.
pages.brief: A female Goliath beetle digs into soft soil, placing eggs in a deep hole. Beside the hole, small larvae have hatched and crawl through the dark earth, chewing bits of dead plants mixed into the soil.

pages.text: Larvae can be as long as your hand. They are as heavy as five mice! As soon as the rain ends, the larvae go deep into the ground. They cover themselves with a thin coat of sand.
pages.brief: A fat white larva stretches across a child's open hand, nearly as long as the hand itself. Around it the soil is dug away, and deeper in the ground other larvae burrow down, bodies coated with thin sand.

pages.text: Larvae change into adult beetles inside the coat of sand. Adults come out when the rain begins again.
pages.brief: Inside a hollow case of packed sand underground, a larva changes into an adult beetle. The adult, striped and shiny, pushes out of the sandy shell as rain soaks the ground above and green leaves hang nearby.

pages.text: A Short Life In zoos, Goliath beetles live to be about eight months old. In the wild, Goliath beetles must find food and escape enemies. They may only live for a few months.
pages.brief: In a zoo enclosure an adult Goliath beetle rests on a branch near a keeper's hand. In another view, a wild beetle climbs a tree trunk while a bird with an open beak swoops close, hunting it.

pages.text: Conclusion People have been studying Goliath beetles for hundreds of years. They are rare and interesting to see. Goliath beetles are amazing insects!
pages.brief: Two people crouch beside a fallen log in an African forest, watching a Goliath beetle through a magnifying glass and sketching it in a notebook. The striped beetle sits on the bark in front of them.

books.title: Goliath Bird-Eating Spiders: Giant Arachnids
books.art_why: The book is about a real spider that exists today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: A Big, Hairy Spider Goliath bird-eating spiders are very big spiders. They are about the size of a dinner plate. They weigh more than any other spider in the world.
pages.brief: A Goliath bird-eating spider, very big and covered in hair, stands on a simple dark surface. Its wide body looks as large as a dinner plate, and its heavy size makes it look like the heaviest spider in the world.

pages.text: Like many spiders, Goliath spiders have eight legs and eight eyes. Even with that many eyes, they can’t see very well. Their bodies are covered with many tiny hairs.
pages.brief: A close view of a Goliath spider shows its eight long legs and eight eyes. Its body is covered with many tiny hairs. The spider looks big and hairy, and its many eyes seem weak for seeing.

pages.text: Two Body Parts Spiders have two body parts. The mouth, fangs, and legs are in the front part. The back part is for making silk.
pages.brief: A close view of a Goliath spider's body shows two main parts. The front part holds the mouth, fangs, and legs. The back part is where the spider makes silk. Its hairy body has a clear front part and back part.

pages.text: A spider with its legs can be about 1 foot (30 cm) across. That’s as long as a ruler!
pages.brief: A Goliath spider spreads its legs wide, reaching about one foot across. A ruler lies beside it to show the same length. The spider's leg span looks as long as the ruler. The hairy spider is seen from above.

pages.text: Home in the Rainforest Goliath spiders live in rainforests. The forests are in hot and wet parts of the world. The spiders make their homes in burrows under the ground.
pages.brief: A Goliath spider stands at the opening of a burrow under the ground. Around it is a hot, wet rainforest with thick green plants. The spider's home is a dark hole in the forest floor.

pages.text: What’s for Dinner? Goliath spiders are great hunters. They hunt at night for mice, insects, and other small prey. The hairs on their body help them sense when a small animal is near.
pages.brief: At night in the rainforest, a Goliath spider hunts near the ground. It moves toward a small mouse and insects, using the tiny hairs on its body to sense them close by. The big spider is ready to catch its prey.

pages.text: When Goliath spiders hunt, they get close to a small animal. Then they grab it with their strong, hairy legs.
pages.brief: A Goliath spider gets very close to a small animal on the rainforest floor. It grabs the animal with its strong, hairy legs. The spider's legs wrap around the prey as it holds on tight.

pages.text: Poison Fangs Giant Goliath spiders have a special weapon. Their fangs are filled with poison. When they bite an animal, the poison makes the animal stop moving. Humans don’t need to worry too much. A bite from a Goliath spider hurts about as much as a wasp sting.
pages.brief: A close view of a Goliath spider shows its large fangs, filled with poison. The spider bites a small animal, and the poison makes the animal stop moving. Nearby, a wasp shows the kind of sting a human bite is compared to.

pages.text: Watch Out for Enemies Even big spiders have enemies. Hawks, owls, and snakes sometimes eat Goliath spiders. An insect called a spider wasp can kill them, too.
pages.brief: A Goliath spider stands on the rainforest floor with enemies nearby. A hawk, an owl, and a snake are around it, and a spider wasp is close by. These animals can eat or kill the big spider.

pages.text: Growing Up Baby spiders hatch from eggs. They look like little adults. They must shed their outside skin to grow bigger. They shed their skin many times during their lives.
pages.brief: Small baby Goliath spiders hatch from eggs and look like little adults. One baby pulls off its outside skin so it can grow bigger. The young spiders stay near the eggs and will shed their skin many times.

pages.text: Learning from Spiders Huge, hairy Goliath spiders are very special. They have an important job in their forest homes. We can learn a lot from them!
pages.brief: A huge, hairy Goliath spider stands in its forest home among rainforest plants. It looks special and important in this place. The big spider is part of the forest, and people can learn a lot from it.

books.title: Incredible Places to Stay
books.art_why: The book shows real hotels and real places that exist today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Incredible Places to Stay.
pages.brief: A dramatic cover image shows a glass sleeping pod suspended high on a rocky mountain face, with snowy peaks and a green valley below, suggesting an incredible place to stay in the wild landscape.

pages.text: World Map of Incredible Hotels 3 INDIAN OCEAN 5 Sala Silvermine Hotel, Sala, Sweden 1 Skylodge Adventure Suites, Cuzco, Peru 6 Jules’ Undersea Lodge, Key Largo, Florida 2 Hôtel de Glace, Quebec, Canada 7 Tundra Lodge, Manitoba, Canada 3 Giraffe Manor, Nairobi, Kenya 4 Treehotel, Harads, Sweden Introduction Do you want to see some of the world’s most amazing hotels? Let’s go!
pages.brief: A colorful world map fills the spread, with small photo windows showing an ice hotel in Canada, a giraffe manor in Kenya, tree houses in Sweden, a mine hotel, an undersea lodge in Florida and a cliff suite in Peru, surrounded by blue oceans.

pages.text: Sky High Your tour starts in the Sacred Valley of Cuzco, Peru. At Skylodge Adventure Suites, you can sleep high in the air.
pages.brief: High above the Sacred Valley in Cuzco, Peru, transparent capsule suites cling to a steep cliff face. A traveler stands on a narrow platform beside one capsule, looking out over the rugged mountains and valley below, ready to sleep high in the air.

pages.text: A Cool Place to Stay The next stop is the Hôtel de Glace (O-tel DEH GLAHS) in Canada. Many parts of the hotel are made of ice.
pages.brief: A grand hotel built from ice and packed snow stands in a snowy Canadian landscape. Visitors in winter coats walk through icy corridors and look at ice-carved rooms, with frozen walls, ice furniture, and soft blue light glowing through clear ice.

pages.text: The ice melts away in the spring. Workers build the hotel again each winter.
pages.brief: In spring sunshine, puddles and melting ice surround the remains of the ice hotel. Later, workers in winter gear rebuild the hotel from blocks of snow and ice, shaping walls and rooms on a snowy site as the next winter approaches.

pages.text: Breakfast with Giraffes From Canada, you’ll travel to Kenya. Giraffes live in the forests around a hotel called Giraffe Manor. Giraffes come to the hotel every morning to eat.
pages.brief: In Kenya, a stately manor house sits among green trees. Several tall giraffes stride out of the forest toward the hotel in the morning light, their long necks reaching toward the building as guests gather to watch them come to eat.

pages.text: If you stay there, you can feed them!
pages.brief: A guest stands on a hotel terrace at Giraffe Manor, holding out food toward a tall giraffe. The giraffe stretches its long neck down to take the treat, while another giraffe waits among the trees behind the manor house.

pages.text: In the Trees The next stop on your tour is Sweden. The Treehotel is made up of many tree houses. The Mirrorcube has glass all around it. This tree house blends in with the woods.
pages.brief: In a Swedish forest, several tree houses are suspended among tall pines. One is a mirrored cube covered in glass, reflecting the trunks and branches around it so it blends into the woods, while sunlight filters through the trees.

pages.text: One tree house looks like a big bird’s nest. The UFO tree house looks like a spaceship from outer space.
pages.brief: Among the forest trees, one tree house is shaped like a giant bird’s nest woven from twigs, and another looks like a silver flying saucer from outer space. Both sit high on trunks, connected by walkways, surrounded by dense green woods.

pages.text: You also stop at the Sala Silvermine Hotel in Sweden. It has the deepest hotel room in the world! It is a long way down to your room. Dress in warm clothes! The mine is cold.
pages.brief: Deep underground in a Swedish silver mine, a hotel room is carved into dark rock. A steep shaft and tunnel lead far down to the room, and a visitor wearing warm clothes walks through the cold, dim passage with a lantern lighting the rocky walls.

pages.text: Sleeping with Fish Your last stop is Jules’ Undersea Lodge in Florida. You have to swim down to reach your room!
pages.brief: Off the coast of Florida, a small undersea lodge rests on the seafloor among clear blue water. A guest in a swimsuit and diving gear swims downward toward the underwater room, passing fish and sunlight filtering through the surface above.

pages.text: You can even order a pizza from your room. Someone from the hotel will swim it down to you.
pages.brief: Inside the underwater lodge, a guest looks out through a round window at fish. Outside, a hotel worker wearing diving gear swims down toward the lodge carrying a pizza in a waterproof case, delivering it to the room beneath the sea.

pages.text: Conclusion It is time to go back home now. All of these hotels are more than just places to stay. Each one is incredible! Polar Bear Fun The Tundra Lodge is in Manitoba, Canada. It looks like a train on big wheels. The hotel moves over the snow to take visitors close to polar bears.
pages.brief: A visitor with luggage leaves an unusual hotel, looking back at the amazing places. Nearby, the Tundra Lodge in Manitoba, Canada, looks like a train on big wheels, moving over snowy ground to bring visitors close to polar bears.

books.title: Cricket
books.art_why: The book includes cricket's 1500s origins and early rules, so drawings suit the historical parts.

pages.text: A Fun Sport People around the world play an exciting sport called cricket. In cricket, a batter hits a ball with a large flat bat. The ball is about the same size as a baseball.
pages.brief: A cricket batter swings a large flat bat to hit a small ball. The ball is about the same size as a baseball. Around the world, people play this exciting sport, and a batter hits the ball during play.

pages.text: The Basics Two teams play a game of cricket. Each team has eleven players. They play on an oval field with an area in the middle. The field is.
pages.brief: Two cricket teams, each with eleven players, stand on an oval field. The field has a special area in the middle where the game is played, and both teams are ready to begin the match.

pages.text: The teams take turns batting and bowling, or throwing, a ball. Two batters on the batting team stand on each end of the pitch. The team that isn’t batting plays in the field.
pages.brief: Two batters from one team stand at opposite ends of the pitch. The other team spreads out in the field around them. The teams take turns batting and bowling, or throwing, the ball during the game.

pages.text: One player on each team is the bowler. The bowler throws a ball to a batter on the other team.
pages.brief: A bowler from one team throws the ball across the pitch toward a batter on the other team. One player on each team is the bowler, and the batter waits with a bat to hit it.

pages.text: The bowler tries to hit three small posts in the ground near the batter. These posts are called stumps. At the top of the stumps are two small pieces of wood called bails. Together, the stumps and bails are If the bowler’s ball knocks the bails off the wicket stumps, the batter is out.
pages.brief: Three small posts stand in the ground near the batter, with two small pieces of wood on top. Together they make the wicket. If the bowler’s ball knocks the top pieces off, the batter is out.

pages.text: The batter protects the wicket by hitting the ball with his or her bat. If the batter hits the ball, he or she runs down the pitch. If the batter swaps places with the other batter, he or she scores one point. The point is called a run.
pages.brief: A batter hits the ball with a bat to protect the wicket, then runs down the pitch. If the batter swaps places with the other batter, the team scores one point. That point is called a run.

pages.text: Nine players on the bowling team play in the field. Their job is to get the balls that the batter hits. They can get the batter out by catching the ball. They can also throw the ball and hit the wicket to get an out. After ten outs, the bowling team gets their turn at bat. At the end of the game, the team with more runs wins.
pages.brief: Nine players from the bowling team spread across the field, ready to get the balls the batter hits. They can catch the ball or throw it to hit the wicket for an out. After ten outs, the teams switch, and the team with more runs wins.

pages.text: The History of Cricket In the 1500s, children in England played cricket. By the early 1700s, adults started playing as professionals. In 1788, people created the cricket rules still in use today.
pages.brief: In England in the 1500s, children play cricket together. By the early 1700s, adults start playing cricket as professionals. In 1788, people create the cricket rules that are still used in the game today, and players follow them.

pages.text: Soon, cricket teams formed outside England as well. Then, people created longer cricket matches called Tests for world.
pages.brief: Cricket teams form outside England as the sport spreads to more places. People create longer cricket matches called Tests for the world. Players from different places take part in these longer games against one another.

pages.text: Cricket teams played once at the Olympic Games in 1900. Some fans hope cricket teams will one day play in every Summer Olympic Games.
pages.brief: Cricket teams play once at the Olympic Games in 1900. Some fans hope cricket teams will one day play in every Summer Olympic Games. Fans around the world watch the games and wish for more Olympic cricket.

pages.text: Cricket Around the World Today, people play cricket around the world. Twelve countries have teams that play in Test matches.
pages.brief: People play cricket around the world today. Twelve countries have teams that play in Test matches. Players from these countries take part in the sport on cricket fields in many different places and enjoy the game.

pages.text: That’s Cricket! Since its start as a children’s game, cricket has been popular. Today, it is followed by billions of fans around the world. You can enjoy cricket, too!
pages.brief: Cricket began as a children’s game and has stayed popular. Today, billions of fans around the world follow cricket. People can enjoy the sport, too, by watching or playing and joining the fans of the game.

books.title: Let's Make Shapes!
books.art_why: A real hands-on drawing activity with paper, pencils and shapes that exists today.

pages.text: Let’s Make Shapes!
pages.brief: A child sits at a table with plain white sheets of paper and bright pencils, drawing a circle, a square, a rectangle and a triangle, the shapes overlapping in a cheerful jumble across the page, ready for making pictures out of them.

pages.text: A line connects two points. A line is longer than it is wide. Lines can be short, and lines can be long. Lines can be straight, and lines can be curved. You can join curved lines together to make a shape. You can join straight lines together to make a shape. You can bend lines to make a shape.
pages.brief: A hand draws on white paper: a short straight line, a long straight line, a wobbly curved line, and a curved line bent round until its ends join into a shape. Beside them, two points are joined by one straight line.

pages.text: There are many kinds of shapes. Circles, squares, rectangles, and triangles are geometric shapes. We can use geometric shapes to draw many things. to make a face. You can use a circle, three small circles, and a curved line When a line goes all the way around, it makes a circle.
pages.brief: On white paper, a circle, a square, a rectangle and a triangle sit side by side. Nearby, a face has been drawn from one big circle, three small circles and a curved line for a smile, showing how lines make shapes and shapes make pictures.

pages.text: On another piece of paper, draw a circle. You can use four half-circles to draw a caterpillar. If we cut a circle in half, we get two half-circles. Then make it a mouse with eyes, ears, and whiskers. Use lines and more circles.
pages.brief: A circle is drawn on paper, then cut in half to make two half-circles. Four half-circles are lined up in a row as a caterpillar. More lines and circles turn another shape into a mouse with eyes, ears and whiskers.

pages.text: On another piece of paper, draw a half-circle. You can use triangles to make a face on a pumpkin. triangle. Triangles have three sides and three corners. When a line turns a corner three times, it makes a Then make it into a fish with eyes, a tail, and fins.
pages.brief: A half-circle lies on the paper and becomes a fish with eyes, a tail and fins. Beside it, triangles make a face on a pumpkin, and one triangle stands alone showing its three sides and three corners, a line turning the corner three times.

pages.text: On another piece of paper, Then make it into a tree draw a triangle. with leaves and a trunk. You can use squares and half-circles to make a truck. Each side is the same length. A square has four sides and four corners. When a line turns a corner four times, it makes a square.
pages.brief: A triangle is drawn, then turned into a tree with leaves and a trunk. Below, squares and half-circles come together as a truck. A single square shows its four equal sides and four corners, a line turning the corner four times.

pages.text: On another Then make it into a dog by adding piece of paper, ears, a tail, and legs. draw a square. Use curved lines and straight lines. to draw a bus. You can use rectangles, circles, squares and lines The other two sides are another length. Two sides are the same length. A rectangle has four sides, just like a square.
pages.brief: A square is drawn, then becomes a dog with added ears, a tail and legs. Curved and straight lines build a bus from rectangles, circles and squares. A rectangle sits beside it, two sides one length and the other two another length.

pages.text: On another piece of paper, draw a rectangle. Then make it a house with a roof, two windows, and a door. Use a triangle and three rectangles. circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles. make a picture using all of the shapes: Now, on another piece of paper.
pages.brief: A rectangle is drawn, then becomes a house with a roof, two windows and a door, built from a triangle and three rectangles. On another sheet of paper, circles, squares, triangles and rectangles are combined into one picture.

books.title: Argentina
books.art_why: Modern Argentina has real places, animals, food, and people that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Where Is It? Argentina is the second-largest country in South America. It is the eighth-largest country in the world. Five countries share borders with Argentina.
pages.brief: A wide view of South America shows Argentina as a very large country in the south, with land borders touching five neighboring countries. The scene emphasizes its size compared with the rest of the continent and the world.

pages.text: About forty-three million people live in Argentina. The capital of Argentina is Buenos Aires. Its name means “fair winds.” About fifteen million people live there.
pages.brief: A busy city view of Buenos Aires shows many people living and moving through the capital. About fifteen million people are suggested by crowded streets, homes, and workplaces, while the country's total population of about forty-three million is represented by the wider city scene.

pages.text: People Most people in Argentina live in big cities. Other people live in the country. Some of these people are farmers. They grow crops such as wheat and grapes.
pages.brief: Farmers work in the countryside, growing crops such as wheat and grapes. In the background, big cities show where most people in Argentina live. The scene contrasts rural farmland with crowded urban areas, with farmers tending rows of plants under open sky.

pages.text: People from all over the world live in Argentina. Many are from Europe. Most people in Argentina speak Spanish.
pages.brief: A diverse group of people from many parts of the world stands together in Argentina. Some faces suggest European origins, and most people speak Spanish. The group is shown in a city or community setting, representing the many backgrounds that make up the country's population.

pages.text: Land Argentina has mountains, lakes, and rivers. The Andes Mountains are in the west. They are the longest group of mountains in the world.
pages.brief: The Andes Mountains rise in western Argentina, with rugged peaks, lakes, and rivers in the landscape. The mountain range stretches far across the land, showing the longest group of mountains in the world. The scene includes high rocky slopes and water below.

pages.text: Argentina has many kinds of animals. Monkeys, wild cats, and many other animals live there. Argentina has some lovely rivers. Some of the river water falls from very high places. The falls are some of the biggest in the world.
