pages.brief: Monkeys, wild cats, and other animals live in Argentina's natural places. A river flows through the scene and drops from very high places, forming huge waterfalls. The animals are shown near the water and forest, with the tall falls in the background.

pages.text: History People have lived in Argentina for thousands of years. Long ago, the Spanish ruled the country. Then, army leaders took control.
pages.brief: Long ago, people lived in Argentina for thousands of years. The scene shows Spanish rulers in the country, followed by army leaders taking control. Historical figures and ordinary people are shown in an old setting, representing the shift in power over time.

pages.text: The army leaders did not let people have any say in their rules. This was unfair for most people. Today, people in Argentina can help make rules. They choose leaders who share their ways of thinking.
pages.brief: People in Argentina today take part in making rules and choosing leaders. A group gathers in a civic setting, sharing ideas and voting. The scene shows fair participation, with leaders and citizens working together, contrasting with earlier unfair rule by army leaders.

pages.text: Celebration One of the biggest parties in Argentina lasts for days. People dress up as clowns and animals. They have a lot of fun. There is music and dancing. There is a big parade.
pages.brief: A big parade fills the streets during one of Argentina's largest celebrations. People dress as clowns and animals, dance to music, and have fun for days. The scene shows a lively crowd, costumes, and dancing in a festive street parade.

pages.text: Food People in Argentina eat meat cooked on a grill. They also eat little pies filled with meat, vegetables, or cheese.
pages.brief: People in Argentina eat meat cooked on a grill and little pies filled with meat, vegetables, or cheese. The scene shows a grill with meat and a tray of small pies on a table, with people gathered to share the food.

pages.text: Conclusion Argentina is a country with people from all over the world. They help to make it a great place with a bright tomorrow.
pages.brief: A bright tomorrow is shown with people from all over the world living together in Argentina. They work and stand together in a hopeful setting, helping to make the country a great place. The scene looks forward with a positive, bright atmosphere.

pages.text: Argentina Population: 43,646,358 Land: 2,736,690 sq km (1,056,642 sq. mi.) Capital City: Buenos Aires Primary Language: Spanish Primary Religion: Roman Catholic Name of Currency: Argentine peso.
pages.brief: A summary view of Argentina shows a large country with a population of about forty-three million, a huge land area, Buenos Aires as the capital, Spanish as the main language, Roman Catholic as the main religion, and the Argentine peso as currency.

books.title: Sled Dogs to the Rescue
books.art_why: A 1925 Alaska event, shown as period illustration rather than modern photo.

pages.text: A Terrible Disease In January 1925, a big storm hit Alaska. Two Native children in a town in Alaska died. Others were very sick and needed medicine.
pages.brief: A small Alaska town under a heavy January snowstorm, wind driving snow past wooden houses. Inside one house, two Native children lie still and quiet, while other children lie sick in bed wrapped in blankets, and worried grown-ups stand close by the beds.

pages.text: The medicine could be brought part of the way by train. There were still 674 miles (1,085 km) to the town.
pages.brief: A steam train pushes through deep snow, its engine dark against white drifts, carrying a small box of medicine part of the way. Beyond the last stop, a long empty snowy track stretches off toward the distant town, hundreds of miles still to travel.

pages.text: Sled dog teams had to bring it the rest of the way.
pages.brief: Teams of sled dogs stand harnessed in the snow, breath steaming, ready to take the medicine onward. Mushers in thick fur parkas and boots check the harness lines and load the small package onto a sled under a grey winter sky.

pages.text: Nome sled dog route railroad The teams raced from the last train stop in Nenana to the town called Nome, where the sick children lived. The Great Sled Dog Relay The medicine came by train and was given to the first team. The race was on. Alaska Nenana GULF OF ALASKA.
pages.brief: A wide snowy view of Alaska: the railroad line coming into Nenana, sled dog teams setting out across the frozen land toward Nome, and the icy Gulf of Alaska coastline far below. Mountains and dark spruce forests fill the distance between the two towns.

pages.text: The medicine was passed from team to team. It often had to be warmed by the fire.
pages.brief: Mushers pass a small wrapped package of medicine from one sled team to the next in the snow. Beside a crackling fire, a driver holds the medicine close to the flames to warm it, dogs resting in harness around him.

pages.text: One driver and his lead dog, Togo, raced for more miles than any other team.
pages.brief: A driver in a fur-lined parka stands on the runners of his sled while his lead dog, Togo, pulls ahead through deep snow at the front of the team, covering more miles than any other team on the route.

pages.text: The Dogs Deliver Another driver and his lead dog, Balto, raced in a blizzard.
pages.brief: Another driver leans into the wind behind his sled as his lead dog, Balto, leads the team through a whirling blizzard, snow blowing hard across the dogs' faces and the trail disappearing into white.

pages.text: At one point, the wind blew them over. The driver had to dig the medicine out of the snow.
pages.brief: Fierce wind knocks the sled and team over in the snow. The driver kneels and digs with his hands in the deep drift, searching for the medicine package buried under the blown snow, dogs struggling to stand nearby.

pages.text: When the last team was not ready to leave, Balto’s team went on instead. Five and a half days after the race began, they made it to the town.
pages.brief: With the next team not ready to leave, Balto's team surges forward on the trail instead, dogs pulling hard through the snow toward the town. Five and a half days after the race began, the team arrives among the town's houses.

pages.text: After the Race After the race, Togo’s team went all over the United States. Balto’s team did, too.
pages.brief: Togo's team and Balto's team travel across the United States, sled dogs standing proudly on show while crowds of people gather to look at them far from the Alaskan snow.

pages.text: Balto’s team lived the rest of their lives in a zoo. Balto was the most famous of the sled dogs.
pages.brief: Balto's team lives out the rest of their lives in a zoo, the dogs resting in an enclosure while visitors watch. Balto stands out among them, the most famous of all the sled dogs.

pages.text: However, the other dogs also helped save the sick children when there was little hope.
pages.brief: The whole line of sled dogs stands together in the snow, drivers beside them, the rescued children well again and standing nearby — every dog honoured for helping save the sick children when there was little hope.

books.title: Amazing Antarctica
books.art_why: Antarctica, its wildlife, scientists, and ships are real-world subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: Amazing Antarctica.
pages.brief: A vast icy Antarctic landscape stretches to the horizon under a pale sky, with frozen ground, snow, and ice as far as the eye can see. The scene feels still and cold, showing the remote continent of Antarctica.

pages.text: North America 2 South America The Seventh Continent You can easily find six continents. Now look at the bottom of the globe. You will find continent number seven. It’s Antarctica!
pages.brief: A globe is seen from the bottom, showing Antarctica at the South Pole beneath the other continents, with the southern oceans around it and the vast white ice of the seventh continent clearly in view.

pages.text: People found Antarctica about two hundred years ago. We have learned a lot about this amazing place.
pages.brief: People in warm expedition clothing stand on a ship deck looking toward icy Antarctic shores, representing the people who found Antarctica about two hundred years ago and began learning about it. The sea is cold and grey.

pages.text: Antarctica is the coldest continent. It also has the strongest winds. Less rain and snow fall there than in other places.
pages.brief: A bleak Antarctic scene shows icy ground and strong wind blowing snow across the surface under a cold pale sky; the land looks dry because very little rain or snow falls there. The wind is fierce.

pages.text: Freezing Antarctica Water covers most of Earth. Almost all of it is salt water. Most of the fresh water is frozen in Antarctica’s ice. Snow does not melt during the summers. The ice builds up over many years.
pages.brief: A wide view of Antarctica’s thick ice sheets beside ocean water shows layers of snow and ice built up over many years under a cold sky, with most fresh water frozen solid in the ice.

pages.text: Life on and Around Antarctica Freezing weather makes Antarctica a dangerous place to live.
pages.brief: A harsh Antarctic landscape of ice and snow stretches under a cold sky, with no shelter in sight; the freezing conditions look dangerous for any plant or animal trying to live there. The place feels empty and severe.

pages.text: Most plants and animals live near or in the sea. There are no trees. There are other plants, such as moss.
pages.brief: A rocky Antarctic shore beside the sea shows patches of green moss growing on stones and small plants near the water; there are no trees, and most life stays close to the sea. The cold water lies nearby.

pages.text: Penguins and seals are some of the larger animals in Antarctica. Wowser! A male emperor penguin has a big job. It takes care of a penguin egg for two months. It does not eat during that time. Then the mother comes back. She feeds the chick.
pages.brief: A male emperor penguin stands on frozen ground, carefully balancing a single egg on his feet as he takes care of it without eating; nearby seals rest near the sea, and a mother penguin returns in the distance.

pages.text: A Playground for Scientists People made sure that scientists can study in Antarctica. Do You Know? No country is in charge of Antarctica. Many countries signed a special agreement in 1961. It does not allow wars to happen in Antarctica.
pages.brief: Scientists in thick cold-weather clothing work outside a small research station on the icy Antarctic surface, showing that people made sure scientists can study there; the scene is calm and focused on research. The station sits alone in the frozen landscape.

pages.text: Many countries send scientists to study in Antarctica. Some work there all year. Others work only in summer.
pages.brief: Scientists from different countries work busily at an Antarctic research base, some dressed for summer and others in heavy winter clothing, with snowy ground and scientific equipment around them as they study through different seasons.

pages.text: Many kinds of scientists come to Antarctica. They study animals and ice. They study many other things.
pages.brief: Several scientists in warm clothing study Antarctic animals and ice, with one observing wildlife and another examining snow and ice near a research camp; they work together to learn many things about the frozen continent.

pages.text: Thousands of visitors also come to Antarctica each year.
pages.brief: A group of visitors in bright cold-weather clothing stands on the deck of a ship near icy Antarctic shores, looking out at the frozen landscape as many thousands of visitors come to Antarctica each year.

pages.text: Conclusion People do not know a lot about Antarctica. The cold, wind, and rough seas make it a hard place to visit. However, people do know it is important to protect Antarctica.
pages.brief: A rough, cold Antarctic seascape shows icy water, strong wind and distant ice; a small ship rides the choppy sea, showing how hard Antarctica is to visit and why people say it is important to protect it.

books.title: The Amazing Octopus
books.art_why: The book is about real ocean animals that exist today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: The A mazing.
pages.brief: A single octopus floats alone in calm, open ocean water, its soft round body and eight long arms spread wide. Sunlight filters gently down through the blue water around it, introducing the amazing sea creature to the reader.

pages.text: Introduction More than three hundred types of octopuses live in ocean waters around the world. Their interesting looks and incredible skills make octopuses amazing creatures of the sea.
pages.brief: Many different octopuses swim in ocean waters around the world, showing a variety of sizes and shapes. Some are large and some are small. Their unusual looks and incredible skills make them stand out as amazing creatures of the sea.

pages.text: How Are Octopuses Born? Mother octopuses watch over their eggs until they hatch. It could take two to twelve months or even longer. Octopus mothers die soon after their eggs hatch.
pages.brief: A mother octopus rests in a rocky den, her body curled protectively around a cluster of eggs. She watches over them in the ocean, staying close through the long months until the eggs finally hatch.

pages.text: What Are Octopuses Like? Octopuses can be big or small. They have two big eyes, a beak, and a soft, round body. They also have eight long arms— each with its own brain! Octopuses have nine brains in total. Near its head, an octopus has a tube called a siphon (SY-fun). An octopus can shoot water, waste, and ink out of its siphon.
pages.brief: An octopus floats in clear ocean water, showing its two large eyes, soft round body, beak, and eight long arms. Near its head, a small tube-like siphon is visible. Water and ink stream out from the siphon.

pages.text: Do You Know? The arms of octopuses are covered with suckers. They help octopuses move around, grab onto rocks, and catch prey. Suckers also let octopuses taste.
pages.brief: A close view of an octopus’s long arm shows rows of round suckers. The suckers grip a rock while the octopus moves along the ocean floor, and the arm curls near prey so the suckers can taste and catch it.

pages.text: They can find their way out of a maze and can even use tools. Octopuses don’t have any bones. They can fit into small spaces. Octopuses are also very smart.
pages.brief: An octopus squeezes its soft, boneless body through a narrow gap between rocks. It can fit into small spaces. Nearby, it uses a small tool with one arm, showing how clever it is. The scene is underwater among rocky crevices.

pages.text: Where Do Octopuses Live? Octopuses usually live in warm water. Some octopuses live in very cold water. Many octopuses like deep ocean waters. Others swim near the ocean’s surface. Scientists found this octopus frozen deep under the ice in Antarctica.
pages.brief: An octopus swims in warm, sunlit water near the ocean’s surface, while another rests in cold, deep water. The scenes show where octopuses can live. Far below Antarctic ice, a scientist examines an octopus found frozen deep under the ice.

pages.text: How Do Octopuses Move? Octopuses can swim fast in an unusual way. First, they take water into their body. Then, they squirt water out of their siphon. The force pushes octopuses backward. Swimming is hard work for octopuses. It’s easier for them to crawl along the ocean floor.
pages.brief: An octopus takes water into its body and squirts it out through its siphon, pushing itself backward through the ocean. In another part of the scene, an octopus crawls more easily along the sandy ocean floor.

pages.text: How Do Octopuses Hunt and Stay Safe? Octopuses hunt fish, snakes, and other ocean animals. Octopuses drop down on their prey. The prey sticks to their suckers. Then octopuses pull their food into their beak.
pages.brief: An octopus drops down from above onto its prey in the ocean. It hunts fish, snakes, and other ocean animals. A fish and a sea snake stick to the suckers on its arms as the octopus pulls the food toward its beak.

pages.text: Predators of octopuses include whales, seals, and large fish. When predators attack, octopuses have different ways to escape. An octopus can bite an attacker and pass on venom.
pages.brief: A whale, a seal, and a large fish surround an octopus in the ocean. These animals are predators of octopuses. The octopus opens its beak and bites one attacker, passing venom, while looking for a way to escape.

pages.text: Octopuses can also shoot dark ink out of their siphon so predators can’t see them.
pages.brief: An octopus shoots a thick cloud of dark ink from its siphon into the surrounding water. The dark cloud spreads around it, hiding the octopus from a nearby predator that cannot see through the murk.

pages.text: Octopuses can even blend in with the colors around them. Then predators can’t see them. Sometimes octopuses get caught. However, if an octopus loses an arm, it can grow a new one!
pages.brief: An octopus blends into the colors of rocks and coral around it, nearly disappearing from view while a predator swims nearby. Sometimes octopuses get caught. One arm is shorter and growing back after being lost.

pages.text: Conclusion Octopuses can do many things. They can swim backward, shoot ink, change colors, and even grow new arms. Octopuses are amazing animals!
pages.brief: An octopus swims backward through the ocean, shoots a burst of ink, and changes color to match its surroundings. A new arm grows where an old one was lost, showing the many amazing things it can do.

books.title: Wonders of Nature
books.art_why: The book is about real animals and their real features.

pages.text: Wonders of Nature.
pages.brief: A wide, colorful nature scene with green plants, water, sky, and a few small wild animals partly hidden among leaves, suggesting many natural wonders without focusing on one named creature. Trees and soft clouds frame the view.

pages.text: Introduction The world is full of interesting animals. Some animals look strange or have special skills. Let’s look at some of these wonders of nature.
pages.brief: A broad view of the natural world shows many interesting animals in different places, some with strange shapes and some showing special skills. The scene suggests a world full of animal wonders, with each creature distinct in its own habitat.

pages.text: Archerfish Archerfish spit water at bugs. The bugs fall into the water, where the archerfish catch and eat them.
pages.brief: An archerfish at the surface of calm water spits a thin stream of water upward at small insects on a low branch. Several bugs fall toward the water, and the archerfish waits below with its mouth ready to catch and eat them.

pages.text: Trap-Door Spider The trap-door spider lives in a tunnel in the ground. Its home has a hidden door made of silk and dirt. The spider hides in its tunnel to hunt.
pages.brief: A trap-door spider waits inside a tunnel in the ground. At the tunnel opening, a round hidden door made of silk and dirt is closed. The spider stays hidden in darkness, ready to hunt from inside its home.

pages.text: Beaver Beavers chew through tree trunks. They make dams out of trees, mud, and stones.
pages.brief: A beaver stands beside a tree trunk, chewing the wood with its teeth. Nearby, a dam built from branches, mud and stones crosses a stream. Cut tree trunks lie around the bank, showing what the beaver uses to build.

pages.text: Chameleon Chameleons change color to hide They even change color to show how they feel.
pages.brief: A chameleon clings to a branch among leaves, its skin color blending with the plants around it. Its body shows a shift in color, suggesting it is hiding or expressing how it feels. No other animal is present.

pages.text: Flying Dragon Flying dragons have skin on their sides that opens like wings. They jump and glide from tree to tree.
pages.brief: A flying dragon lizard spreads the skin flaps along its sides like wings as it jumps from one tree branch. It glides through the air between trees, with its wide skin membrane open and its legs held out.

pages.text: Leaf Insect The body parts of leaf insects look just like leaves. These animals blend in well with real leaves on trees.
pages.brief: A leaf insect rests among real leaves on a tree, its body parts shaped and colored like leaves. Its legs and body blend closely with the surrounding foliage, making it hard to tell the insect from the real leaves.

pages.text: Leaf- Rolling Weevil The female leaf-rolling weevil rolls a leaf into She lays her eggs inside the The leaf hides and protects her eggs.
pages.brief: A female leaf-rolling weevil works on a leaf, rolling it into a tight tube. She lays her eggs inside the rolled leaf. The curled leaf wraps around the eggs, hiding and protecting them as they stay inside.

pages.text: Praying Mantis The praying mantis holds its front legs in a praying position. A mantis has five eyes to help it hunt for food.
pages.brief: A praying mantis holds its front legs folded in a praying position while standing on a leafy plant. Its head faces forward with five eyes visible, helping it search for food. The insect looks alert and ready to hunt.

pages.text: Mole Moles dig tunnels to find and eat worms. These animals have tiny eyes, but they are not blind.
pages.brief: A mole digs through soil in a tunnel underground, its small front paws pushing dirt aside. A worm is nearby in the earth. The mole’s tiny eyes are visible on its face, showing that it is not blind.

pages.text: Sea Dragon Sea dragons are small fish. They look like ocean plants. Their leafy parts help them catch food and hide from enemies.
pages.brief: A sea dragon, a small fish, floats among ocean plants. Its leafy parts make it look like seaweed, helping it hide from enemies and catch food. The fish’s body blends with the plant shapes around it.

pages.text: Conclusion Interesting animals come in many shapes and sizes. They are all wonders of nature.
pages.brief: A varied group of interesting animals of different shapes and sizes appears together in a natural setting, representing many kinds of animal wonders. Some are large, some small, each distinct and shown as part of the natural world.

books.title: Ocean Animals
books.art_why: Ocean mammals, fish and reptiles exist today, so real photographs are possible.

pages.text: Many kinds of animals live in the ocean. They are part of the ocean community. Most of the ones in this book are mammals, fish, or reptiles. Let’s meet some of these ocean animals.
pages.brief: A wide underwater view of the open ocean where many kinds of animals swim together — several fish, a marine mammal and a sea turtle sharing the same blue water, showing the different animals that make up the ocean community.

pages.text: I have a sleek body and a strong tail to swim fast. I live in a group called a pod, and I like to eat fish. I whistle to talk to other dolphins. My thick layer of fat keeps me warm. I live on ice and in cold water. I use them to dig for clams and to protect myself. I am a walrus, and I have ivory tusks.
pages.brief: A sleek dolphin with a strong tail swims fast among other dolphins in its pod, fish nearby. On ice beside cold water, a walrus with long ivory tusks rests, its thick fat layer visible, tusks ready for digging clams.

pages.text: I am a hammerhead shark, and my head has a very funny shape. My eyes and nostrils are at the ends of lobes. I like to eat fish. I bark like a dog, and I am covered by short fur. I eat squid, octopus, and fish. I am smart, noisy, and playful. I am a California sea lion.
pages.brief: A hammerhead shark with its wide, funny-shaped head swims after fish, eyes and nostrils at the ends of its lobes. Nearby, a California sea lion with short fur is noisy and playful among squid, octopus and fish.

pages.text: I am an octopus. I have a soft body and no skeleton. I have eight arms with suckers. I shoot black ink from my body to hide and escape from danger. I can also change the color of my skin. I eat seals, dolphins, and fish. that are shaped like triangles. I have very sharp teeth I am a large and fierce shark. I am a great white shark.
pages.brief: An octopus with a soft body and eight sucker-covered arms shoots a cloud of black ink while its skin changes color. A large great white shark swims close by, mouth open to show rows of very sharp, triangular teeth.

pages.text: I have fins that look like wings. I am related to stingrays, but I do not sting. carry eggs until they hatch. not females, Male sea horses, favorite food. Shrimp are my to hide. I change color but I am not.
pages.brief: A seahorse with fins like small wings hovers among seagrass, its skin changing color to hide, tiny shrimp drifting nearby. A male seahorse carries a pouch of eggs, waiting for them to hatch.

pages.text: I lay eggs on land. Jellyfish are my favorite food. I am covered with leathery skin instead of a shell. I eat tiny animals called krill. I make deep sounds that move through water. I am the largest mammal ever to live.
pages.brief: A huge leatherback sea turtle with leathery skin instead of a shell is on land, laying eggs, a jellyfish floating in the water nearby. Out in the ocean, a blue whale feeds on tiny krill and makes deep sounds through the water.

pages.text: The ocean is home to all these animals. Many of them are endangered. They all suffer because of pollution and hunting. books.title: Firefighters
books.art_why: Modern firefighters, trucks, tools and training all exist today and are photographed constantly; only one line mentions long-ago city fires.

pages.text: Introduction Have you ever heard a fire truck racing to a fire? Firefighters put out fires and save lives. They help keep fires from starting. They teach people about fire safety.
pages.brief: A red fire truck races down a city street with lights flashing, while at a fire scene firefighters in helmets and heavy coats spray water on a burning building and later stand talking with a group of people about fire safety.

pages.text: What Makes Fire Burn Fires need air to burn. They also need fuel. Wood and oil are two kinds of fuel. The more fuel, the hotter the fire will be. But even a candle flame burns very hot. Do You Know? In our solar system, Earth is the only planet where fire can burn. Earth is the only planet with enough oxygen. Oxygen is a gas in the air.
pages.brief: A candle burns with a bright flame on a table beside a stack of wood and a can of oil. Above, a view of Earth from space shows the blue planet wrapped in white clouds and the air that holds its oxygen.

pages.text: Kinds of Fires Firefighters put out fires in houses and tall buildings. They also fight forest fires. They must be ready to put out many kinds of fires.
pages.brief: Three fire scenes side by side: firefighters pouring water on a burning house, others climbing inside a tall building on a ladder, and a line of firefighters facing a wall of flame in a forest of trees.

pages.text: Firefighting Tools Firefighters use many different tools. They use hoses to spray water or foam on fires. They break down doors with axes. They use ladders to reach high places.
pages.brief: Firefighters at work with their tools: one grips a thick hose spraying water and white foam, another swings an axe at a closed door, and a third climbs a ladder propped against a high window.

pages.text: Smoke masks protect firefighters from smoke. Fans move smoke from rooms. Fire extinguishers can put out small fires.
pages.brief: A firefighter wears a smoke mask over the face inside a smoky room. Beside them a large fan blows the grey smoke out through an open doorway, and a hand aims a small red fire extinguisher at a small flame.

pages.text: Firefighting Machines Fire trucks are important firefighting machines. A fire engine has a pump to spray water.
pages.brief: A shiny red fire engine parked at the scene, its pump running, sends a powerful stream of water from a hose onto a burning building while firefighters stand on the ground guiding it.

pages.text: Ladder trucks carry ladders. Tanker trucks carry water. Rescue trucks carry tools to help trapped people.
pages.brief: Three trucks shown clearly: a ladder truck with long ladders raised high, a tanker truck full of water, and a rescue truck with its doors open, firefighters lifting tools out to reach people trapped inside a damaged building.

pages.text: Other kinds of machines fight fires, too. Fireboats fight fires from the water. Helicopters drop water on fires. Planes help put out forest fires, too.
pages.brief: A fireboat on the water sprays a fountain of water at a burning pier, a helicopter hovers overhead dropping water from a bucket, and a plane flies low over a forest releasing a long trail of water.

pages.text: Becoming a Firefighter Firefighters must be at least eighteen years old. They must be strong and in good shape. They must also pass a written test.
pages.brief: A strong, fit young adult runs and lifts equipment outdoors, then sits at a table with a paper test in front of them, a pen in hand, working through the written questions to become a firefighter.

pages.text: Firefighters go to school for training. They learn how to fight different kinds of fires. They also learn how to treat hurt people.
pages.brief: Firefighter trainees in a training yard practise putting out a controlled fire with hoses, while in another part of the school a trainee kneels beside a hurt person, learning how to treat injuries and help them.

pages.text: Conclusion Fire is useful, of course. People have used it to cook and stay warm for many thousands of years. At the same time, fire can be very dangerous. Fires take many lives and destroy forests.
pages.brief: A cooking pot sits over a small fire and a family warms their hands at a campfire. Beyond them, a fierce fire tears through a forest, flames leaping up the trunks and destroying the trees.

pages.text: Fires also destroy thousands of buildings every year. Long ago, fires burned down entire cities. Today, firefighters put out fires and keep us safe.
pages.brief: Blackened ruins of burnt buildings stand in rows. Beside them an old painting-style view of a whole city in flames long ago, then today's firefighters in helmets putting out a fire and keeping people safe.

books.title: Garrett Morgan and the Traffic Signal
books.art_why: The book is about a named famous person, Garrett Morgan, so cartoon fits the biography style.

pages.text: Garrett Morgan and the Traffic Signal.
pages.brief: A portrait-style view of Garrett Morgan standing beside a tall traffic signal. He looks calmly toward the viewer. The signal stands beside him. The scene introduces the inventor and the signal in a clear, simple composition.

pages.text: Traffic Problems In the 1920s, the streets were getting very busy. Many things shared the streets.
pages.brief: A busy 1920s city street filled with many different kinds of traffic sharing the same road. The street looks crowded and active. Several travelers and vehicles are close together. The scene shows that the streets were getting very busy.

pages.text: Cars were on the streets. Horses and buggies were on the streets. People and bikes were on the streets, too.
pages.brief: Cars move along a 1920s street while horses and buggies travel beside them. People walk and bicycles ride along the same road. All of them share the busy street together. The scene shows the many kinds of traffic.

pages.text: A man named Garrett Morgan lived in Cleveland, Ohio. He saw a car on the street hit a horse and buggy. He saw that the streets were not safe.
pages.brief: Garrett Morgan stands on a Cleveland, Ohio street and watches a car hit a horse and buggy. He sees the crash happen in front of him. The street looks unsafe. Mr. Morgan’s face shows concern as he observes the accident.

pages.text: Making a Plan Each day more traffic was on the streets. Mr. Morgan knew there would be more traffic problems. He thought about how to solve these problems.
pages.brief: Garrett Morgan stands near a busy street and thinks about the growing traffic. More cars and other traffic fill the road each day. He looks thoughtful as he considers the traffic problems. He is working out how to solve them.

pages.text: Mr. Morgan knew Cleveland needed a way to help the traffic. He thought about how to do this. He made a plan for a traffic signal.
pages.brief: Garrett Morgan sits with a plan for a traffic signal. He thinks about what Cleveland needs to help its traffic. He studies the idea in his mind. The scene shows him making a plan for a new traffic signal.

pages.text: The Traffic Signal The traffic signal had arms. The arms went up and down.
pages.brief: A close view of Garrett Morgan’s traffic signal. It has long arms that move up and down. The signal stands at a street location. The arms are shown in raised and lowered positions. The signal is the new invention.

pages.text: Later, traffic signals used lights. The lights told traffic when to stop and when to go.
pages.brief: Later traffic signals use lights to guide traffic. A signal with lights shows when cars should stop and when they should go. Cars wait at a stop and then move forward. The lights help control the traffic.

pages.text: Mr. Morgan’s traffic signal could also stop all traffic. Then it was safe for people to cross the street.
pages.brief: Garrett Morgan’s traffic signal stops all traffic at once. With every vehicle halted, people can cross the street safely. Pedestrians walk across while cars wait. The signal makes a safe moment for people to cross. The scene shows how the signal protects people crossing.

pages.text: The traffic signal was put on street corners. It was easy to make traffic stop and go at corners. Mr. Morgan’s plan worked!
pages.brief: The traffic signal stands on a street corner. Cars stop and go as the signal directs them. It is easy to control traffic at the corner. Mr. Morgan’s plan works well in the busy street.

pages.text: The Man with the Plan Garrett Morgan made the streets safe for people, cars, and horses and buggies.
pages.brief: Garrett Morgan stands beside a safe street where people, cars, and horses and buggies share the road. The traffic moves without danger. He looks satisfied with the safer streets. The scene shows the man who made the streets safe.

pages.text: Mr. Morgan also made other things. He made a mask to help keep firefighters safe. He also started a newspaper in Cleveland.
pages.brief: Garrett Morgan holds a mask made to keep firefighters safe. Beside him is a newspaper he started in Cleveland. He stands with these other creations. The scene shows more of Mr. Morgan’s work beyond the traffic signal.

pages.text: Mr. Morgan was a problem solver. He saw a problem. He looked for a way to solve it.
pages.brief: Garrett Morgan looks at a problem and searches for a way to solve it. He is a problem solver who thinks carefully. He watches, considers, and finds answers. The scene shows him using his mind to make things better.

books.title: What Pet Should You Get?
books.art_why: Real pets and children can be photographed today.

pages.text: J Should You Get? What Pet What Pet Should You Get?
pages.brief: A smiling child sits cross-legged in a bright room, chin on hand, thinking about choosing a pet. A calm dog, a small lizard, a fish in a bowl and a colorful parrot are spaced around the child, each shown clearly as a possible pet.

pages.text: Introduction Almost every kid has wanted Pets can make good friends. But how do you decide which kind of pet to get?
pages.brief: A young child sits on a rug in a cozy home, hugging a friendly pet and smiling. Two other children nearby watch with eager faces, showing that many kids have wanted pets and that pets can be good friends. The child looks thoughtful about choosing a kind.

pages.text: Here are some kids who have some opinions about pets. Read what they have to say. Then decide what kind of pet you would like to have.
pages.brief: Several children sit around a table in a bright room, each with a thoughtful expression about pets. One child leans forward to share an opinion, another listens, and a third looks unsure. Their faces show different views as they compare choices.

pages.text: Dogs as Pets Every kid should own a dog. A dog comes when you call it. You know it likes you because it wags its tail. Dogs like to play chase with you. Some dogs will even play catch!
pages.brief: A happy child stands in a grassy yard, calling a dog that runs toward them with its tail wagging. The dog looks eager to play. Nearby, the child tosses a ball for catch, and the dog is ready to chase.

pages.text: Dogs as Pets Dogs are hard pets to keep. They need lots of space to run. What if you don’t have a yard? You have to take them on walks even if it is cold. The worst thing is that you have to clean up after them. Yuck, who wants a dog?
pages.brief: A child walks a dog on a leash along a cold, windy street, bundled in a coat. The dog pulls forward, needing space to run. Back home, the child frowns while cleaning up after the dog, looking unhappy about the chore.

pages.text: Lizards as Pets Lizards make the coolest pets. They don’t bark or meow. You don’t have to take them for walks. They are easy to hold and to pet. It doesn’t cost much for lizard food. So, go get a lizard!
pages.brief: A smiling child sits on a sofa in a bright room, gently holding a small lizard in both hands. The lizard rests calmly, with no leash nearby. A small dish of food sits on a side table, showing an easy, low-cost pet.

pages.text: Lizards as Pets It is mean to keep lizards as pets. Some have to stay in one tiny box their whole life. Some of them eat live crickets. Plus, it feels really weird to pet them. Never, ever, get a lizard!
pages.brief: A lizard sits inside a tiny glass box on a table, with little room to move. Beside it, a container holds live crickets. A child reaches toward the lizard but pulls their hand back with a weirded-out face.

pages.text: Fish as Pets Fish make awesome pets. They come in such pretty colors. It is fun to watch them swim back and forth. It is fun to watch their funny mouths. They only need to be fed once a day. Fish make fun and easy pets to keep.
pages.brief: A child leans close to a fish tank in a cozy room, watching colorful fish swim back and forth. The fish have funny mouths, and the child smiles at them. A small pinch of food is dropped in once.

pages.text: Fish as Pets Fish should be left in the oceans and rivers. Fish don’t come when you call them. They can’t do any tricks. And worse than that, fish don’t like to be touched. Fish win the most boring pet award.
pages.brief: A child stands by a river and calls to fish swimming in the water, but the fish ignore the call and swim away. Another child reaches toward the water, yet the fish stay out of reach. The fish do no tricks.

pages.text: Parrots as Pets One of the best pets to own is a parrot. Parrots are very beautiful birds. They often do not need a cage. I love it when my parrot says “hello.” Some parrots even whistle. Get a parrot and teach it to talk.
pages.brief: A child sits in a sunny room with a colorful parrot perched on their arm, no cage around it. The parrot opens its beak as if saying hello, and the child smiles. Nearby, the parrot lifts its head to whistle.

pages.text: Parrots as Pets Parrots are really messy pets. They spill seeds and fruit all over. They are not the best drinkers. They get water on the floor. Their feathers can even fall out. Don’t get a parrot unless you like cleaning!
pages.brief: A messy room shows a parrot on a perch with seeds and fruit spilled across the floor. A tipped water bowl sends water onto the floor, and loose feathers lie nearby. A child kneels with a cloth, cleaning up.

pages.text: Conclusion There are good things and bad things about each pet. You have to decide whether the good things are great. You have to decide whether the bad things are okay for you.
pages.brief: A thoughtful child sits at a table in a bright room, looking at a dog, a lizard, a fishbowl and a parrot arranged nearby. The child's face shows careful weighing, as if thinking about good things and bad things for each pet.

pages.text: You also have to do research to see whether your house is good for a pet. Don’t get a pet unless you have thought hard about it. But the right pet can be your best friend!
pages.brief: A child and a parent stand in a home, looking around the rooms and checking whether there is good space for a pet. The child holds a notebook and thinks hard. Later, the child hugs a pet closely as a best friend.
